Will this API change break a client?

Keep the client fixed and change the API. See why valid JSON alone does not guarantee compatibility.

The existing client sends { "title": "Review API contract" } to POST /demo/tasks. It expects 201 Created, reads id and title as strings, and ignores extra response fields.

The client stays fixed while the API changes. PASS means its expectation still holds; FAIL means it breaks; NOT RUN means an earlier check stopped it. Apply compatible rollout to compare a migration that preserves this client. Highlighted JSON lines differ from the original response.

Compatible with this client · Client decoding. Client reads task-42: Review API contract.

This client ignores fields it does not read, so adding priority leaves its existing behaviour intact.

  • PASS · Old request accepted
  • PASS · id remains a string
  • PASS · title remains a string
Original API

Required request fields: title

201 Created

{
  "id": "task-42",
  "title": "Review API contract"
}
Changed API

Required request fields: title

201 Created

{
  "id": "task-42",
  "title": "Review API contract",
  "priority": "normal"
}

Safer rollout: Keep the added field optional for consumers; check stricter clients separately.

What makes the other changes break?
  • Rename title to name: the client no longer finds the title it reads.
  • Change id to a number: the client expects a string, so decoding fails.
  • Require priority in the request: the old request omits it, so validation returns 400 before the client can read a task.

These results apply to the client defined above. A stricter client could reject extra fields; other clients may tolerate different changes. Review actual consumers before changing a real API.

DECISION /demo/articles/draft-42Fictional publishing workspace

Signed in does not mean allowed.

Can this person act on this record? Change the context to inspect the decision.

Change any selection to re-evaluate immediately. Workspace is the record’s location relative to the user’s assignment. Checks run in order: identity, workspace, permission, record state. STOP blocks the operation; NOT RUN marks later checks. Even an administrator is limited to the assigned workspace.

BLOCK · 403 Forbidden. Reviewer and editor roles cannot publish in this example.

  1. PASS · IdentityA fictional signed-in identity is present.
  2. PASS · WorkspaceThe record belongs to the assigned workspace.
  3. STOP · PermissionReviewer and editor roles cannot publish in this example.
  4. NOT RUN · Record stateAn earlier check stopped the operation.

Stopped before the operation. No read or write.

Read the fictional policy

Signed-in reviewers, editors and administrators may read records in their assigned workspace. Only administrators may publish drafts there. No role can access another workspace or publish archived records. Missing or unknown context permits no operation.

Illustrative browser model with no real accounts, requests or saved changes. The displayed checks explain this example; they are not an API response or real security enforcement. Real services must validate permissions on every request, on the server. OWASP guidance (opens in a new tab).

Find a route

Same grid, different search strategy. Compare breadth-first search (BFS) with depth-first search (DFS).

BFS explores in layers using a queue; DFS follows a branch using a stack. Explored counts visited cells. Pending counts discovered cells awaiting exploration. Route moves counts steps in the resulting route, not all visited cells. Run animates the search; Next step inspects one visited cell.

BFS explores in layers; DFS follows a branch before backtracking.

Route moves
—

BFS uses a queue. With equally weighted moves, its first route to the goal is a shortest route. DFS uses a stack and can find a longer route.

Moves have equal cost: up, right, down or left. Walls cannot be crossed. This deterministic example runs entirely in your browser.

Read the search trace and comparison

BFS takes the oldest pending cell; DFS takes the newest. Neighbours are considered up, right, down, left. The choice changes both the route and how much of the board is explored. Neither algorithm is always faster on every board.

In the two-route example, the shortest route takes 8 moves through the lower passage. Following the upper branch takes 12 moves. A blocked goal has no route.
